newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lyonnais - a bank from rags to riches, to rags.
newsitem.headline: Lyonnais - a bank from rags to riches, to rags.

text.p: France's Credit Lyonnais is still suffering a hangover from the binge of expansion and investment which made it the world's biggest bank outside Japan for a spell during the financial boomtime 1980s.

The creaking "grand old lady" of French banking is now turning once again to the government to help it out of trouble after several costly rescues. The government announced on Friday the latest bailout plan, which it had promised to present to the European Commission for approval this week, would not be submitted until late March.
Following are some key dates in the bank's history:

1863 - Founded by Henri Germain, the 39-year-old son of a silk merchant, in the French provincial city of Lyon. 1865 - Opening of the first branch in Paris. 1870 - The seige of Paris during the Franco-Prussian war prompts the bank to open one of its first foreign branches in London. 1945 - Nationalised by government decree after World War Two along with Banque Nationale de Paris and Societe Generale, the three "grand old ladies" of French banking. 1988 - Jean-Yves Haberer, a top civil servant with close ties to the Socialist party, named chairman. He sets out to fulfil Socialist party ambition of creating giant French banking group capable of competing on the world stage. 1990 - Bank reports record profits of 3.71 billion francs. 1990 - The bank's Dutch subsidiary, CLBN, financed Italian financier Giancarlo Parretti's $1.3 billion bid for Hollywood film studio MGM. 1991 - Bank reports profits of 3.16 billion francs. 1992 - Credit Lyonnais gets into the movie-making business, taking control of MGM after Parretti defaults on loan payments. 1992 - Bank reports 1.85 billion franc loss. 1993 - Chairman Jean-Yves Haberer is removed in November and replaced by Jean Peyrelevade, former chairman of insurer Union des Assurances de Paris. Haberer pushed across into far less prestigious job at Credit National. 1993 - Bank suffers loss of 6.9 billion francs, one of the largest in French corporate history at the time. 1994 - March 24 - Government unveils rescue package with an ultimate cost of 23.3 billion francs to the French taxpayer, including cash injection of 4.9 billion francs. March 30 - Government fires Haberer from Credit National and opens inquiry to pinpoint how Credit Lyonnais ran up enormous losses. September 27 - Bank announces 1994 first-half loss of 4.49 billion and says state has postponed plans for a second rescue package until Spring 1995. 1995 March 17 - Bank reports 1994 loss of 12.1 billion francs and government 20-year rescue plan is announced which involves spinning off net assets worth about 135 billion francs from its balance sheet to a new unit to be called Consortium de Realisation. Assets to be shed include its MGM film studio. Initial estimates by then finance minister Edmond Alphandary put the asset sale losses at some 50 billion francs. July 30 - European Commission approves rescue package in return for pledge to sell off 35 percent of Credit Lyonnais assets outside France by the end of 1998 and a pledge to privatise the bank around the turn of the century.

1996 March 21 - Bank reports 1995 profit of 13 million francs but highlights that it still strained by cost of funding the state company handling its asset sales under the May 5 - Fire destroys 19th Century headquarters of Credit Lyonnais in Boulevard des Italiens, Paris. July 17 - MGM Hollywood studio sold for $1.3 billion to group led by U.S. billionaire Kirk Kerkorian and Australia's Seven Network TV firm. Oct 3 - Bank reports profit of 67 million francs for first half of 1996, with help of European Commission-approved emergency aid from government to tune of 3.9 billion francs; says will need more state funds because financing terms of 1995 rescue package dragging it down. Dec 2 - Paris public prosecutor opens criminal investigation, requested by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, into suspected fraud and the issuing of misleading financial information in early 1990s. 1997 - Government holds negotiations with European Commission on new rescue package which some newspaper reports estimate could cost up to 30 billion francs. Government due to present its rescue package in February.

Rival Societe Generale says it will challenge rescue package at European Court of Justice in Luxembourg and demands the government consider a "controlled liquidation" of the bank. Feb 21 - Government postpones to end March plan to present rescue package to European Commission after Brussels demands changes to outline. After throwing the bank open to bids last September, it says it does not expect the bank to be able to be privatised for another two years.
